title: Data Literacy & Wrangling

character.name: The Data Janitor
character.tagline: 80% of AI is mopping up messy data. I brought two mops.

oneLiner: Garbage in, garbage out: how to clean, split, and respect your data before modeling.
analogy: Data is like ingredients delivered to a restaurant in a chaotic pile — some rotten, some mislabeled, some in the wrong units (is that grams or pounds?!). Before you cook (train), you sort, wash, and taste. And crucially, you hide a portion of the ingredients in a locked fridge (the test set) so you can honestly check whether tonight's dish works on food the chef has never seen. Sneaking a peek at that fridge while cooking is cheating — it's called data leakage.
objectives: Understand why data quality matters more than model choice for most projects.
Split data into train / validation / test and know what each is for.
Spot common data problems: missing values, imbalance, leakage, and bias.
Grasp what 'features' are and why feature quality drives results.
keyConcepts: Garbage in, garbage out: models learn whatever patterns (and mistakes) live in the data.
Split data into training (learn), validation (tune), and test (final honest check) sets — never train on the test set.
Data leakage is when information from the test set (or the future) sneaks into training, giving fake-good results.
Class imbalance (e.g. 99% 'not fraud') can make accuracy misleading; you may need resampling or better metrics.
Features are the input columns the model sees; good feature engineering often beats a fancier model.

keyTerms.plain: An input column — a measurable property the model learns from.
Three data piles: learn, tune, and a locked fridge for honest grading.
Accidentally letting the model peek at the answers. Fake-good scores.
When one outcome is way rarer than another, skewing naive accuracy.
The correct answer attached to a training example.

scenarios.scenario: A fraud model reports 99.4% accuracy and everyone celebrates. Then you notice only 0.6% of transactions are actually fraud, and the model flags almost nothing.
scenarios.question: What's really going on?

options.label: Class imbalance — the model 'wins' by always predicting 'not fraud,' so accuracy is misleading
The model is perfect and should ship immediately
There is too little math in the model

scenarios.explanation: With heavy imbalance, predicting the majority class gives high accuracy while catching zero fraud. Use precision/recall/F1 and techniques for imbalance instead of raw accuracy.

scenarios.scenario: A teammate scaled and imputed missing values using statistics computed over the ENTIRE dataset, then split into train and test.
scenarios.question: Why is this a problem?

options.label: It causes data leakage — test-set information influenced preprocessing, inflating results

scenarios.explanation: Preprocessing statistics must be learned on the training set only, then applied to validation/test. Fitting on all data leaks test information and overstates performance.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the test set?
options: To give an honest final estimate of performance on unseen data
quiz.answer: To give an honest final estimate of performance on unseen data
quiz.explanation: The test set is the locked fridge — used once at the end for an unbiased performance estimate. Tuning happens on the validation set.

quiz.question: 'Garbage in, garbage out' means:
options: Model quality is limited by the quality of the training data
quiz.answer: Model quality is limited by the quality of the training data
quiz.explanation: Models learn from data; flawed, biased, or noisy data produces flawed models regardless of architecture.

quiz.question: What is data leakage?
options: When information not legitimately available at prediction time sneaks into training
quiz.answer: When information not legitimately available at prediction time sneaks into training
quiz.explanation: Leakage (e.g. using future data or test statistics during training) produces impressive scores that collapse in production.

quiz.question: Why can accuracy be misleading on an imbalanced dataset?
options: A model can score high by always predicting the majority class while missing the rare, important cases
quiz.answer: A model can score high by always predicting the majority class while missing the rare, important cases
quiz.explanation: On a 99/1 split, predicting the majority yields 99% accuracy yet catches none of the 1% you care about. Use precision/recall/F1.

quiz.question: In ML, a 'feature' is:
options: An input variable/column the model uses to make predictions
quiz.answer: An input variable/column the model uses to make predictions
quiz.explanation: Features are the inputs. Thoughtful feature engineering frequently improves results more than swapping models.
